cards.name: Glaucoma
short: A progressive eye disease: the eye pressure rises and the optic nerve is damaged; the goal is to decrease the pressure.
Open angle: the aqueous humor does not drain well, and there are no symptoms at first. Angle closure: tied to the shape of the eye, painful, an emergency.
Inflow is the making of aqueous humor by the ciliary body; outflow is its drainage (trabecular meshwork and Schlemm’s canal, or uveoscleral).

Decrease inflow: beta receptor antagonists, alpha 2 agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. Increase outflow: M3 agonists, the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, prostaglandin agonists, the Rho kinase inhibitor.
After an eye drop, press the inner corner of the eyelid so less drug is absorbed into the body.

steps.title: What it is, and the two types
steps.q: What separates primary open-angle from primary angle-closure glaucoma, and what is the goal of treatment?

rows: A progressive eye disease. The pressure inside the eye, the [[iop|intraocular pressure (IOP)]], rises, and the {{optic nerve}} is damaged; vision is lost
{{Decrease the IOP}}, which delays or prevents disease progression
The drainage systems not working effectively: the aqueous humor cannot drain out as it should
Usually {{gradual and asymptomatic}} until visual field loss occurs
The eye doctor measures the IOP; a pressure that climbs from the person’s baseline is rechecked sooner
The {{shape of the eye}} and how it sits in the eye socket (slide 13)
A {{medical emergency}}: the IOP must be decreased quickly

The slide ties it to the shape of the eye. In lecture the closed angle was also described as the outflow area closing after a blow to the eye with swelling, or a chemical exposure; the pressure rises very quickly and can damage the nerve

items: ★ The objectives of this lecture include classifying drugs as production inhibitors or outflow enhancers (slide 11)

steps.title: Aqueous humor: inflow and outflow
steps.q: Where is aqueous humor made, by which two routes does it leave, and which receptors and enzyme sit in the ciliary body?

rows: The [[ciliary-body|ciliary body]] (a ring behind the iris, with smooth muscle) makes [[aqueous-humor|aqueous humor]] all the time
Ciliary body → {{posterior chamber}} (between the lens and the iris)
Out of the anterior chamber through the {{angle}}
The {{drainage}} of aqueous humor out of the eye
Through the [[trabecular-meshwork|trabecular meshwork]], a spongy tissue
Most of the aqueous humor leaves this way
[[uveoscleral|Uveoscleral]] outflow: between the uvea and the sclera
If the aqueous humor does not drain, the pressure builds in the anterior chamber and is transferred toward the optic nerve, damaging it

blocks.text: Receptors and enzymes in the ciliary body and meshwork (slide 16)

rows: Blood vessels of the ciliary body
{{M3}} (muscarinic) receptors, and maybe some beta 2 receptors

items: How the receptors lead to aqueous humor is not fully known. The role of carbonic anhydrase is understood better.
Agonizing the beta receptors gave more aqueous humor; antagonizing them gave less. That led to the beta receptor antagonists.
Beta antagonists, alpha 2 agonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors decrease the production of aqueous humor.

steps.title: Treat it: does the drug decrease inflow or increase outflow?
steps.q: For each class, is it a production inhibitor or an outflow enhancer, and what does it act on?

blocks.title: Inflow or outflow
rows: Decrease inflow (brimonidine also increases uveoscleral outflow)
Increase outflow, mainly uveoscleral; no effect on inflow
Increase outflow through the trabecular meshwork

blocks.label: Decrease inflow
blocks.title: Beta receptor antagonists
pts: Block the beta-adrenergic receptor on the ciliary body: {{less aqueous humor is made}}
{{Not much effect on outflow}}; the mechanism is not fully understood
Timolol, levobunolol, betaxolol, carteolol

blocks.label: Decrease inflow
blocks.title: Alpha 2 agonists
pts: Bind alpha 2 receptors on the ciliary body: {{decrease the rate of aqueous humor production}}
Brimonidine has two extra effects: it {{increases uveoscleral outflow}} and is {{neuroprotective}} (seen in animals)
pick: Preventing a rise in IOP after eye surgery such as cataract surgery

blocks.label: Decrease inflow
blocks.title: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
pts: Inhibit carbonic anhydrase: less carbonic acid, so less sodium and bicarbonate to secrete and {{less aqueous humor}}
Oral: acetazolamide, methazolamide. Ophthalmic: dorzolamide, brinzolamide
pick: The patient is refractory to other therapies
An oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor is added

blocks.label: Increase outflow
blocks.title: M3 agonists
pts: Agonize the M3 receptor on the sphincter muscle and the trabecular meshwork: they contract and {{outflow increases}}
Carbachol, pilocarpine
pick: Longer duration, less allergic reaction in the eye
More potential for an allergic reaction in the eye

blocks.label: Increase outflow
blocks.title: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor
pts: {{Irreversible}} inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase: more acetylcholine, the same contraction and increase in outflow
Used when a patient is refractory to other glaucoma medicines

blocks.label: Increase outflow
blocks.title: Prostaglandin agonists
pts: Agonize the {{PGF2α receptor}}: the ciliary muscle relaxes
Increase uveoscleral outflow and, to a lesser extent, trabecular outflow; they do {{not affect production}}
May be more effective in hazel or brown eyes than in blue or green eyes

blocks.label: Increase outflow
blocks.title: Rho kinase inhibitor
pts: Inhibits {{RhoA kinase}}: the trabecular meshwork relaxes (less stiff, fewer fibrosis-related proteins), so outflow increases

blocks.label: Two mechanisms
blocks.title: Combination products
pts: Timolol/dorzolamide, timolol/brimonidine, brinzolamide/brimonidine, latanoprost/netarsudil
Treatment often starts with one drug and moves to a combination as the disease progresses; one product replaces two

steps.title: Side effects, and what to tell the patient
steps.q: Which side effect goes with each class, why does a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor cause metabolic acidosis, and what lowers systemic absorption?

blocks.title: Side effect to know for each class
rows: Systemic: bradycardia, hypotension; bronchospasm in asthmatics (beta 2 blocked). Ocular: stinging, burning, decreased night vision
Allergic reaction in the eye; systemic hypotension
Foreign body sensation and itching of the eyes; oral dryness, dizziness, fatigue, somnolence, lower blood pressure and pulse
Oral: {{metabolic acidosis}}, increased urination, dry mouth, thirst, altered taste and smell, depression. Ocular drops: burning, stinging, bitter taste
Painful ciliary muscle spasm (headache), blurred vision, myopia; diarrhea, salivation, sweating, rhinorrhea
Brow ache, twitching of the eyelids, allergic type reaction, {{cataracts}}; the same systemic effects
Increased brown pigmentation of the iris and eyelids; longer, thicker lashes; hair growth in other areas
Conjunctival hyperemia (53%); corneal verticillata, instillation site pain, conjunctival hemorrhage (about 20%)

blocks.text: ★ Why a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor causes metabolic acidosis (kidney, proximal tubule)

rows: Carbonic anhydrase makes carbonic acid, which splits into {{hydrogen ion}} and {{bicarbonate}}
Leaves the cell in exchange for sodium coming in
Leaves with sodium into the blood and {{buffers the blood pH}}
No carbonic acid, so no hydrogen ion to exchange for sodium: sodium and water stay in the lumen (more urine). No bicarbonate reaches the blood
The blood pH falls: {{metabolic acidosis}}, most important with the oral drugs
No bicarbonate is made in the ciliary body cells, so it is not secreted, water does not follow, and aqueous humor decreases

items: ★ After the drop, gently press the inner corner of the eyelid: the drug then does not drain through the tear duct into the nose, whose lining is highly vascularized, and is not absorbed into the bloodstream
Some glaucoma drops have cardiovascular effects, and older patients with glaucoma may already have heart conditions
For a cardiac patient on a beta receptor antagonist: a more selective drug, or the eyelid compression

patients.t: A man with asthma and open-angle glaucoma is started on a drop that blocks beta receptors on the ciliary body.
patients.q: Which problem is most likely if the drug is absorbed into the body?
o: Darkened iris, because PGF2α receptors are stimulated
Bronchospasm, since airway beta 2 receptors are blocked
Metabolic acidosis, because carbonic acid is no longer made
Diarrhea and salivation, because M3 receptors are stimulated
patients.w: Beta receptor antagonists that block beta 2 receptors can cause bronchospasm in asthmatics (slide 20).

x.Metabolic acidosis, because carbonic aci: That is the carbonic anhydrase inhibitor effect.
x.Diarrhea and salivation, because M3 rece: Those are M3 agonist and acetylcholinesterase inhibitor effects.
x.Darkened iris, because PGF2α receptors a: That is a prostaglandin agonist effect.

patients.t: A woman with heart disease uses timolol drops. She asks what she can do to keep less of the drug from entering her body.
o: Blink several times right after each drop
Take the drop at night instead of in the morning
Close the eye tightly for a minute and then open it
Press the inner corner of the eye after each drop
patients.w: Compressing the inner corner stops the drug draining through the tear duct into the nose, where it would be absorbed (11/13, 11/17).

x.Blink several times right after each dro: Blinking pushes tears into the puncta and down the tear duct, which carries the drug toward the nose.
x.Take the drop at night instead of in the: The lecture’s point is to stop the drainage through the duct; the time of day does not do that.
x.Close the eye tightly for a minute and t: Closing the eye does not block the duct at the inner corner; compression does.

patients.t: A patient with refractory glaucoma is started on oral acetazolamide.
patients.q: Which effect needs monitoring, and why does it happen?
o: Metabolic acidosis: less bicarbonate reaches the blood
Bronchospasm: beta 2 receptors in the airways are blocked
Conjunctival hyperemia: vascular smooth muscle relaxes
patients.w: Without carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule cells, bicarbonate is not formed and not sent to the blood, so the blood pH falls (11/17).

x.Bronchospasm: beta 2 receptors in the ai: That is a beta receptor antagonist effect.

patients.t: After some weeks on a glaucoma drop, a woman has darker brown eyelids, a darker iris and longer lashes.
patients.w: Prostaglandin agonists increase the brown pigmentation of the iris and eyelids and the lashes (slide 39).

x.Rho kinase inhibitor: Netarsudil causes conjunctival hyperemia, not pigmentation.
x.Alpha 2 agonist: Alpha 2 agonists cause foreign body sensation, itching and dryness of the mouth, not pigmentation.
x.Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor: Ophthalmic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors cause burning, stinging and a bitter taste.

patients.t: A man with chronic open-angle glaucoma needs an alpha 2 agonist for long-term use.
patients.q: Which one is the better choice?
patients.w: Brimonidine is the better long-term choice; apraclonidine tends to cause an allergic type response and is used to prevent a rise in IOP after eye surgery (11/13, slide 23).

x.Apraclonidine: It is used after eye surgery such as cataract surgery; its allergic response limits long-term use.
x.Carbachol: It is an M3 agonist, not an alpha 2 agonist.
x.Echothiophate: It is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, not an alpha 2 agonist.

cards.name: Allergic conjunctivitis
short: Antigen binds IgE on a [[mast-cell|mast cell]]; histamine is released and causes itching, swelling and redness.
Ophthalmic antihistamines are H1 inverse agonists; most also stabilize mast cells.
Mast cell stabilization prevents the release, so those drugs can be started before exposure; cetirizine does not have it.
Alpha 2 agonists are vasoconstrictors: they reduce redness and edema.
The combination product is naphazoline with pheniramine.

steps.title: What happens: histamine from mast cells
steps.q: How does an allergen lead to itchy, red, swollen eyes?

rows: Histamine is stored in {{granules}} in mast cells
Antigen interacts with {{IgE}} on the mast cell surface
The mast cell degranulates: {{histamine}} and other inflammatory cytokines are released
Histamine has a central role in immediate hypersensitivity and allergic responses
{{Itching}} and secretion from the nasal mucosa
Relaxes small blood vessels; formation of {{edema}}
Contracts the bronchi and gut through {{H1 receptors}}
In the CNS, H1 activation inhibits appetite and increases wakefulness
Edema, itch, inflammation and watery eyes (slide 52); redness (slide 56)
Bacterial and viral conjunctivitis; this lecture covers allergic conjunctivitis only (T@39661 11/17)

items: The objectives: list the symptoms; explain the mechanism of each class; know which class treats which symptom; list the side effects (slide 47)

steps.title: Ophthalmic H1 inverse agonists (antihistamines)
steps.q: What are the two mechanisms of these drugs, why does the second one matter, and which drug lacks it?

rows: {{H1 inverse agonist}}: [[inverse-agonist|reduces the constitutive activity]] of the receptor and competes with histamine for it
[[mcs|Mast cell stabilization]]: {{reduces the release}} of mast cell mediators during an allergic response
Anti-inflammatory: less cytokine secretion, less adhesion molecule expression, inhibition of eosinophil infiltration
H1 receptor dependent and independent mechanisms; how it works is still unclear
Reduces {{edema, itch, inflammation and watery eyes}}
Drugs with mast cell stabilization may be {{more effective topically}}

blocks.label: Prevention
blocks.title: Start before exposure
pts: Histamine is harder to stop once it has been released; a mast cell stabilizer started before the allergen season stops the release
If histamine is released anyway, the H1 inverse agonism is also present
★ {{Cetirizine}} has no mast cell stabilization, so it is not the one suggested for prophylactic use

rows: H1 inverse agonist and mast cell stabilization
{{H4 receptor}} antagonism (on eosinophils; may explain its superiority)
Very little anticholinergic activity; little CNS penetration; low incidence of side effects
H1 inverse agonist and mast cell stabilization
Also a nasal spray for allergic rhinitis
A little anticholinergic activity and it penetrates the CNS (11/17)
H1 inverse agonist and mast cell stabilizer
Minimal anticholinergic effects; negligible CNS penetration, but still causes {{drowsiness}}
H1 inverse agonist and mast cell stabilization
Also an {{H2 antagonist}}, which may reduce eyelid edema
H1 inverse agonist and mast cell stabilizer
H1 inverse agonist and mast cell stabilization
Also a nasal spray for allergic rhinitis

steps.title: Alpha 2 agonists, the combination, and which class for which symptom
steps.q: What do the alpha 2 agonists do in the eye, and which class treats which symptom?

rows: Adrenergic receptor agonists: {{vasoconstrictors}} for local application to the nasal mucous membrane or the eye
Less leaking from the capillaries, so less edema
Naphazoline, oxymetazoline, tetrahydrozoline, brimonidine tartrate, phenylephrine
Little difference between them for allergic conjunctivitis when used topically
{{Naphazoline/pheniramine}}: an alpha 2 agonist with an antihistamine
One drop covers vessel constriction, antihistamine action and mast cell stabilization rather than two separate drops

blocks.title: Which class for which symptom
rows: Antihistamines; alpha 2 agonists also reduce the leaking

blocks.label: Alpha 2 agonist
blocks.title: Brimonidine for the eye
pts: The same drug that decreases inflow in glaucoma; here it is a vasoconstrictor that reduces redness

patients.t: A woman has itchy, watery eyes every spring and wants a drop she can start before the pollen season to prevent the itch.
patients.q: Which property of an ophthalmic antihistamine fits this?
o: H2 antagonism, which may reduce eyelid swelling in allergy

patients.w: Cetirizine is an H1 inverse agonist without mast cell stabilization (slide 53; 11/17).

patients.t: A man with allergic conjunctivitis says swollen eyelids bother him most.
patients.q: Which ophthalmic antihistamine also blocks H2 receptors, which may reduce eyelid edema?
patients.w: Epinastine is also an H2 antagonist, which may reduce eyelid edema (slide 54).

x.Alcaftadine: Its extra action is H4 receptor antagonism.
x.Azelastine: It is also used as a nasal spray for allergic rhinitis.

patients.t: A woman has itchy eyes and very red eyes, and would like one drop that both constricts the vessels and acts as an antihistamine.
patients.w: The combination of an alpha 2 agonist with an antihistamine is naphazoline/pheniramine (slide 59).

patients.t: A student is worried about side effects from an ophthalmic antihistamine and asks which one has little CNS penetration and a low incidence of side effects.
patients.w: Alcaftadine has very little anticholinergic activity, little CNS penetration and a low incidence of side effects (slide 53).

x.Cetirizine: Its CNS penetration is negligible, but it still causes drowsiness.
x.Epinastine: Its feature is the H2 antagonism that may reduce eyelid edema.

cards.name: Dry eye
short: [[ksc|Keratoconjunctivitis sicca]]: inflammation reduces tear production; common, with age and female gender as risk factors.
The prescription drugs are not first line; they act on the inflammation.
Cyclosporine: a calcineurin inhibitor; blocks IL-2 production. Loteprednol: a corticosteroid.
Lifitegrast: blocks LFA-1 binding to ICAM-1. Contact lenses out before the drop, back in after 15 minutes.
Intranasal varenicline: a nicotinic receptor agonist that increases tear production through the trigeminal nerve.

steps.title: What it is, who gets it, and the tear film
steps.q: What is the pathology of dry eye, who gets it, and what are the three layers of tears?

rows: One of the most common eye complaints; prevalence {{7% to 33%}}
Often unpredictable; may correlate with the environment
Antihistamines, decongestants, antidepressants, hormone replacement therapy
May present {{with or without}} redness of the eyes
Lubricating drops come first; the prescription drugs below are not first line
Lipids, from the {{meibomian glands}} at the eyelid margin
Aqueous, from the main and accessory lacrimal glands; about {{98%}} of the tear film
Mucins, from the {{goblet cells}} in the conjunctiva
Nutrients, enzymes and immunoglobulins that support and protect the cornea

steps.title: Treat it: four mechanisms
steps.q: What does each prescription drug act on?

blocks.title: What each drug acts on
rows: Calcineurin: less IL-2 made, so less T-cell proliferation and less inflammation
Corticosteroid: gene expression changes, fewer inflammatory genes and more anti-inflammatory genes
LFA-1 on leukocytes: blocks its interaction with ICAM-1, so less adhesion and cytokine secretion
Nicotinic receptor agonist: activates the trigeminal parasympathetic pathway; more basal tear film

blocks.label: Calcineurin inhibitor
blocks.title: Cyclosporine, topical
pts: Increases tear production in patients whose tear production is suppressed by ocular inflammation from keratoconjunctivitis sicca
Binds [[cyclophilin|cyclophilin]]; that complex inhibits calcineurin, so IL-2 is not made. Tacrolimus binds [[fkbp|FKBP]] instead
Acts in the signal cascade, not at signal 1 or signal 2
Used topically: {{oral cyclosporine}} is a significant immunosuppressant (risk of opportunistic infections)

blocks.label: Corticosteroid
blocks.title: Loteprednol, topical
pts: Used for its anti-inflammatory properties to treat dry eye
The corticosteroid for dry eye; not every skin steroid is used

blocks.label: LFA-1 antagonist
blocks.title: Lifitegrast
pts: A [[lfa-1|lymphocyte function-associated antigen 1 (LFA-1)]] antagonist: blocks LFA-1 binding to {{ICAM-1}}
{{1 drop}} in each eye {{twice daily}}, about every 12 hours

blocks.label: Nicotinic agonist
blocks.title: Intranasal varenicline
pts: A nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist; a {{nasal spray}}
{{One spray in each nostril}} twice daily, about 12 hours apart

steps.title: Side effects, and what to tell the patient
steps.q: Which side effect and which counseling point goes with each drug?

blocks.title: Side effects
rows: Ocular burning, instillation site pain, conjunctival hyperemia, discharge, epiphora, eye pain, foreign body sensation, pruritus, stinging, visual disturbances
Application site irritation (5% to 25%); reduced visual acuity (5% to 25%)
Acquired night blindness (rare), blurred vision (infrequent), retinal vascular disorder (rare), subcapsular cataract (rare), transient blindness (rare), visual disturbance (infrequent)

items: ★ Lifitegrast: remove contact lenses before the drop and reinsert them {{15 minutes}} after; it can discolor contact lenses
Intranasal varenicline: originally a smoking cessation drug; FDA licensed the 0.03-mg nasal spray for dry eye in the second half of 2021
Acquired night blindness with the spray is rare; she said it is a reason for the patient to stop using it

beta-blockers.name: Beta receptor antagonists (timolol, levobunolol, betaxolol, carteolol)

sm.text: Block the beta-adrenergic receptor on the ciliary body, so less aqueous humor is made (inflow falls); not much effect on outflow; the mechanism is not fully understood. Timolol and levobunolol: nonspecific beta blockers (levobunolol has some alpha-adrenergic effects). Betaxolol: relatively beta 1 selective. Carteolol: nonspecific with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity. Side effects: ocular stinging and burning, decreased corneal sensitivity, diplopia, blurred or cloudy vision, decreased night vision, ptosis; systemic bradycardia and hypotension, bronchospasm in asthmatics, headache, insomnia, taste perversion, depression, impotence.

how.text: Block the beta-adrenergic receptor on the ciliary body, so less aqueous humor is made (inflow falls); not much effect on outflow; the mechanism is not fully understood. Timolol and levobunolol: nonspecific beta blockers (levobunolol has some alpha-adrenergic effects). Betaxolol: relatively beta 1 selective. Carteolol: nonspecific with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity. Side effects: ocular stinging and burning, decreased corneal sensitivity, diplopia, blurred or cloudy vision, decreased night vision, ptosis; systemic bradycardia and hypotension, bronchospasm in asthmatics, headache, insomnia, taste perversion, depression, impotence.

counsel: After the drop, gently press the inner corner of the eyelid (by the nose) so the drug does not drain through the tear duct and is absorbed into the body.
Timolol comes as a gel that is given once a day; the other drops are given several times a day.
Effectiveness is similar across the group; the choice can rest on side effects or insurance coverage.
avoid: Asthma: beta 2 blockade can cause bronchospasm (slide 20)
Cardiac patients: bradycardia and hypotension (slide 20); a more selective drug, or the eyelid compression (11/13)
Levobunolol may be more effective than timolol and betaxolol after cataract surgery (11/13)

apraclonidine.name: Apraclonidine

sm.text: An alpha 2 agonist: binds alpha 2 receptors on the ciliary body and decreases aqueous humor production (inflow). Used to prevent a rise in IOP after eye surgery such as cataract surgery; not used long term because of an allergic type response. Side effects: ocular burning and stinging, blurred vision, foreign body sensation, ocular pruritus; systemic hypotension, oral dryness, allergic reaction.

how.text: An alpha 2 agonist: binds alpha 2 receptors on the ciliary body and decreases aqueous humor production (inflow). Used to prevent a rise in IOP after eye surgery such as cataract surgery; not used long term because of an allergic type response. Side effects: ocular burning and stinging, blurred vision, foreign body sensation, ocular pruritus; systemic hypotension, oral dryness, allergic reaction.

counsel: After the drop, gently press the inner corner of the eyelid (by the nose) so the drug does not drain through the tear duct and is absorbed into the body.

brimonidine.name: Brimonidine

sm.text: An alpha 2 agonist: binds alpha 2 receptors on the ciliary body and decreases aqueous humor production (inflow). Two extra effects: it increases uveoscleral outflow and is neuroprotective (seen in animals, assumed in humans). The better choice for long-term glaucoma treatment. Side effects: foreign body sensation and itching of the eyes (a hallmark); systemic oral dryness, dizziness, fatigue, somnolence, lower blood pressure and pulse. For allergic conjunctivitis: an alpha 2 agonist vasoconstrictor that reduces redness (brimonidine tartrate).

how.text: An alpha 2 agonist: binds alpha 2 receptors on the ciliary body and decreases aqueous humor production (inflow). Two extra effects: it increases uveoscleral outflow and is neuroprotective (seen in animals, assumed in humans). The better choice for long-term glaucoma treatment. Side effects: foreign body sensation and itching of the eyes (a hallmark); systemic oral dryness, dizziness, fatigue, somnolence, lower blood pressure and pulse. For allergic conjunctivitis: an alpha 2 agonist vasoconstrictor that reduces redness (brimonidine tartrate).

pa.role: Glaucoma (Dr. Smith, Exam 3): decreases aqueous humor production; also increases uveoscleral outflow; neuroprotective
pa.how: The better long-term alpha 2 agonist than apraclonidine.

pa.role: Allergic conjunctivitis (Dr. Smith, Exam 3): alpha 2 agonist vasoconstrictor; reduces redness
pa.how: Brimonidine tartrate is on the list with naphazoline, oxymetazoline, tetrahydrozoline and phenylephrine.

counsel: Glaucoma: After the drop, gently press the inner corner of the eyelid (by the nose) so the drug does not drain through the tear duct and is absorbed into the body.
Allergic conjunctivitis: it constricts the blood vessels in the eye, which reduces redness.
avoid: Foreign body sensation and itching of the eyes are the notable ocular effects (11/13)

cai.name: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, methazolamide, dorzolamide, brinzolamide)

sm.text: Inhibit carbonic anhydrase, which prevents the conversion of CO2 and water to carbonic acid; less sodium and bicarbonate are available for secretion, so the ciliary body makes less aqueous humor (inflow falls). Acetazolamide and methazolamide are oral; dorzolamide and brinzolamide are ophthalmic. Side effects of the drops: burning or stinging, hypersensitivity, headache, bitter, sour or unusual taste, dry eye, foreign body sensation, blurred vision. Oral: altered taste and smell, dry mouth, excessive thirst, increased urination, systemic acidosis, depression.

m3-agonists.name: M3 agonists (carbachol, pilocarpine)

sm.text: Direct-acting parasympathomimetics: agonists at the M3 receptor on the sphincter muscle and the trabecular meshwork; contraction increases outflow. Carbachol is very potent and longer acting, and is used more often; pilocarpine has more potential for an allergic reaction in the eye. Side effects: burning and stinging; painful ciliary muscle spasm causing headache; blurred vision, myopia, poor vision in dim light, floaters, lacrimation; systemic diarrhea, salivation, sweating, rhinorrhea.

echothiophate.name: Echothiophate

sm.text: An irreversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor: more acetylcholine agonizes the M3 receptors, the sphincter muscle and trabecular meshwork contract, and outflow increases. Used when a patient is refractory to other medicines. Side effects: burning and stinging, blurred vision, eye pain, lacrimation, headache, brow ache, twitching of the eyelids, an allergic type reaction (more than pilocarpine), cataracts; systemic diarrhea, salivation, sweating, rhinorrhea.

pg-agonists.name: Prostaglandin agonists (bimatoprost, latanoprost, latanoprostene bunod, travoprost, tafluprost)

sm.text: Agonists at the PGF2α receptor, which relaxes the ciliary muscle; IOP falls by increasing uveoscleral outflow and, to a lesser extent, trabecular outflow. They do not affect aqueous humor production. May be more effective in hazel or brown eyes than in blue or green eyes. Latanoprostene bunod is also a nitric oxide donor (vasodilation adds to its effect). Side effects: blurred vision, burning and stinging, eye pain, lid edema, ocular hyperemia; increased brown pigmentation of the iris and eyelids; hypertrichosis and hyperpigmentation of the lashes (Latisse); hair growth in other areas; few systemic effects.

netarsudil.name: Netarsudil

sm.text: Inhibits RhoA kinase. RhoA is a GTP-binding protein that regulates cell shape, motility, proliferation and apoptosis; in glaucoma it may increase contractile tone and trabecular meshwork stiffness. Inhibiting it lowers outflow resistance: it relaxes the tone, decreases fibrosis-related protein deposits in the meshwork and changes the permeability of the cells lining Schlemm’s canal. The only Rho kinase inhibitor on the drug list. Side effects: conjunctival hyperemia (53%), from vasodilation; about 20%: corneal verticillata (vision unchanged, resolved on stopping in most cases), instillation site pain, conjunctival hemorrhage.

glaucoma-combos.name: Glaucoma combination products

sm.text: Timolol and dorzolamide; timolol and brimonidine; brinzolamide and brimonidine; latanoprost and netarsudil. Treatment often starts with one drug and moves to a combination as the disease progresses. One product with both mechanisms replaces two bottles.

how.text: Each product joins two of the mechanisms above: a beta receptor antagonist, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, an alpha 2 agonist, a prostaglandin agonist or the Rho kinase inhibitor.

counsel: A drop that has to be used 3 or 4 times a day is easier to follow as one combination product than as two separate drops.
After the drop, gently press the inner corner of the eyelid (by the nose) so the drug does not drain through the tear duct and is absorbed into the body.

ophthalmic-h1.name: Ophthalmic H1 inverse agonists (antihistamines)

sm.text: H1 inverse agonists: reduce the constitutive activity of the receptor and compete with histamine for it. Most also stabilize mast cells, which reduces the release of mast cell mediators and is anti-inflammatory (less cytokine secretion, less adhesion molecule expression, inhibition of eosinophil infiltration). Mast cell stabilization may make them more effective topically. They reduce edema, itch, inflammation and watery eyes. Examples: alcaftadine, azelastine, bepotastine, cetirizine, epinastine, ketotifen, olopatadine; cetirizine has no mast cell stabilization.

cetirizine-eye.name: Cetirizine (ophthalmic)

sm.text: H1 inverse agonist without mast cell stabilization. Minimal anticholinergic effects and negligible CNS penetration, but it still causes drowsiness.

alpha2-eye.name: Alpha 2 agonist vasoconstrictors (naphazoline, oxymetazoline, tetrahydrozoline, brimonidine tartrate, phenylephrine)

sm.text: Adrenergic receptor agonists: vasoconstrictors for local application to the nasal mucous membrane or the eye. They reduce redness, and less leaking from the capillaries reduces edema. Little difference between them for allergic conjunctivitis.

cyclosporine.name: Cyclosporine

sm.text: Binds cyclophilin; the complex inhibits calcineurin, so IL-2 is not made for T-cell proliferation. Topical cyclosporine increases tear production where it is suppressed by ocular inflammation from keratoconjunctivitis sicca. Side effects: ocular burning, instillation site pain, conjunctival hyperemia, discharge, epiphora, eye pain, foreign body sensation, pruritus, stinging, visual disturbances.

sm.text: A topical corticosteroid used for its anti-inflammatory properties to treat dry eye. Corticosteroids change gene expression: fewer inflammatory genes and more anti-inflammatory genes are expressed, so the immune response decreases.

lifitegrast.name: Lifitegrast

sm.text: A lymphocyte function-associated antigen 1 (LFA-1) antagonist. LFA-1 is a cell surface protein on leukocytes; lifitegrast binds it and blocks its interaction with intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1), which may inhibit T-cell adhesion to ICAM-1 and the secretion of inflammatory cytokines. 1 drop in each eye twice daily, about every 12 hours. Side effects: application site irritation (5% to 25%), reduced visual acuity (5% to 25%).

varenicline.name: Intranasal varenicline

sm.text: A nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist. In dry eye its effect is thought to come from agonist activity at nicotinic receptors that activates the trigeminal parasympathetic pathway, so basal tear film increases. Originally a smoking cessation drug; the 0.03-mg intranasal spray was licensed for dry eye in the final half of 2021. One spray in each nostril twice daily, about 12 hours apart. Side effects: acquired night blindness (rare), blurred vision (infrequent), retinal vascular disorder (rare), subcapsular cataract (rare), transient blindness (rare), visual disturbance (infrequent).

iop: The pressure inside the eyeball. In glaucoma it increases, and over time it can damage the optic nerve.
aqueous-humor: The liquid the ciliary body makes all the time. It fills the anterior chamber and drains out of the eye through the angle.
ciliary-body: A ring behind the iris, with smooth muscle and blood vessels. It holds the lens by ligaments and makes the aqueous humor.
trabecular-meshwork: A spongy, porous tissue around the opening of Schlemm’s canal. Most aqueous humor leaves through it into the canal, and then the veins.
uveoscleral: The smaller outflow route: aqueous humor squeezes between the uvea (ciliary body, its ligaments and the iris) and the sclera.
mast-cell: A cell that stores histamine in granules. Antigen interacting with IgE on its surface releases the histamine.
inverse-agonist: The activity a receptor has on its own. An inverse agonist reduces it, and also competes with the natural ligand (histamine at H1).
mcs: Reduces the release of mast cell mediators during an allergic response and is anti-inflammatory. How it works is still unclear.
ksc: The name for dry eye: inflammation with reduced tear production.
cyclophilin: The protein cyclosporine binds; the cyclosporine–cyclophilin complex inhibits calcineurin.
lfa-1: Lymphocyte function-associated antigen 1: a cell surface protein on leukocytes that interacts with ICAM-1.

a: No, and the onset is gradual → next question

path.q: Is it tied to drainage that does not work well, or to the shape of the eye?
a: The drainage does not work well → **open angle**
The shape of the eye and how it sits in the socket → **angle closure**

The shape of the eye and how it sits in the eye socket
{{Gradual}} and asymptomatic until visual field loss
Found by measuring the IOP at eye exams
Both: the goal is to decrease the IOP to delay or prevent progression.

tell.title: Glaucoma drugs: decrease inflow or increase outflow

path.q: Does the drug change how much aqueous humor the ciliary body makes?
a: Yes → **inflow**: beta receptor antagonists, alpha 2 agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors

path.q: Does it act on the trabecular meshwork or the ciliary muscle?
a: Yes → **outflow**: M3 agonists, acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, prostaglandin agonists, Rho kinase inhibitor

rows: Beta receptor antagonists; alpha 2 agonists; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
M3 agonists; acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; prostaglandin agonists; Rho kinase inhibitor
Beta receptors, alpha 2 receptors, carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body epithelium
M3 receptors and acetylcholinesterase (trabecular meshwork), PGF2α receptor (ciliary muscle), RhoA kinase
Prostaglandin agonists: mainly uveoscleral outflow; they do not affect production
Beta receptor antagonists have not much effect on outflow.

pairs.title: Brimonidine or apraclonidine?
a: long-term choice; also increases uveoscleral outflow; neuroprotective; foreign body sensation and itching
b: prevents a rise in IOP after eye surgery; allergic type response limits long-term use
pairs.same: Both are alpha 2 agonists that decrease aqueous humor production.
profs: Brimonidine is the better long-term choice (slide 23; T@51660 11/13).

pairs.title: Carbachol or pilocarpine?
a: very potent; longer duration; less allergenic; used more
b: more potential for an allergic reaction in the eye
pairs.same: Both are direct-acting M3 agonists that increase outflow.
profs: Slide 31 lists both; the differences are from lecture (T@26432, T@26752 11/17).

pairs.title: M3 agonist or acetylcholinesterase inhibitor?
a: act like acetylcholine at the M3 receptor
b: irreversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor: more acetylcholine; refractory cases; cataracts
pairs.same: Both parasympathomimetics contract the sphincter muscle and trabecular meshwork and increase outflow; both can cause diarrhea, salivation, sweating and rhinorrhea.

pairs.title: Timolol or betaxolol?
a: nonspecific beta blocker; gel form once a day
pairs.same: Both block the beta receptor on the ciliary body and decrease inflow; efficacy is similar across the group.
profs: Slide 19; T@45583, T@46338 11/13. Levobunolol has some alpha-adrenergic effects; carteolol has intrinsic sympathomimetic activity.

pairs.title: Cyclosporine or tacrolimus: which protein does it bind?
pairs.same: Each complex inhibits calcineurin, so IL-2 is not expressed; both act in the signal cascade.
profs: Slide 66; T@60561 11/17. She said she asked this on purpose because the proteins return in oncology.

pairs.title: Cetirizine or the other ophthalmic antihistamines?
a: H1 inverse agonist only; drowsiness; not suggested for prophylaxis
b: Alcaftadine, azelastine, bepotastine, epinastine, ketotifen, olopatadine
H1 inverse agonist plus mast cell stabilization
pairs.same: All are ophthalmic H1 inverse agonists that reduce itch, edema, inflammation and watery eyes.

pairs.title: Oral or ophthalmic carbonic anhydrase inhibitor?
a: oral; metabolic acidosis and diuresis effects
b: ophthalmic; used first; burning, stinging, bitter taste
pairs.same: Both inhibit carbonic anhydrase and decrease aqueous humor production.
